title: The subject participle
intro: Turkish has no relative pronouns like **who**, **which** or **that**. To describe a noun by an action, it turns the verb into an adjective and puts it in front of the noun: *kitap okuyan kız*, the girl who is reading a book. This unit covers `-(y)An`, the participle of the doer: before a noun, as a noun on its own (*gelenler*, those who came), with a possessed subject (*babası doktor olan çocuk*, the child whose father is a doctor), the order of everything that comes before a noun, and the older aorist participles that live on in everyday words (*çalar saat*, *çıkmaz sokak*).

blocks.text: `-(y)An` (two-way harmony, with the buffer y after a vowel) turns a verb into an adjective: *okumak* → *okuyan* (reading, who reads), *gelmek* → *gelen* (coming, who came). The participle takes its whole clause with it, objects and place words included, and the clause goes before the noun.

blocks.label: From a sentence to a noun phrase
lines: Kız kitap okuyor.       The girl is reading a book.
kitap okuyan kız        the girl who is reading a book
Adam kapıda bekliyor.   The man is waiting at the door.
kapıda bekleyen adam    the man waiting at the door

blocks.text: The noun after the participle is always its **subject**: the girl reads, the man waits. For **the book that the girl is reading**, where the noun is the object, Turkish uses a different participle, `-DIk`, which comes in [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik).

blocks.caption: Forming `-(y)An`
head: Verb
Participle
Example
rows: *İzmir'den gelen tren*, the train from Izmir
*gazete okuyan adam*, the man reading a newspaper
*otobüs bekleyen yolcular*, passengers waiting for the bus
*Taksim'e giden otobüs*, the bus going to Taksim
*yardım eden komşu*, the neighbour who helped
*dondurma yiyen çocuk*, the child eating an ice cream
*evet diyen herkes*, everyone who says yes
*gelmeyen öğrenciler*, the students who didn't come

blocks.text: The stems change as they do before `-(I)yor` ([A1 unit 6](gp-present-continuous)): *git-* and *et-* soften to *gid-*, *ed-*; *ye-* and *de-* become *yi-*, *di-* before the buffer y. The negative is `-mA` + y + `-An`: *gelmeyen*, *okumayan*.

**Time.** `-(y)An` has no tense of its own; the sentence and the time words supply it. *Şimdi konuşan kadın* is **the woman who is speaking now**, *dün gelen mektup* **the letter that came yesterday**, *Türkçe bilen biri* **someone who knows Turkish**. For the future, the next unit gives `-(y)AcAk`.

items.tr: Kitap okuyan kız benim kız kardeşim.
items.seg: Kitap oku|y|an kız benim kız kardeşim.
items.en: The girl reading a book is my sister.
Who's the man waiting at the door?

items.tr: Bu otobüs Taksim'e giden otobüs mü?
items.seg: Bu otobüs Taksim'e gid|en otobüs mü?
items.en: Is this the bus that goes to Taksim?
The train from Izmir is late.
The woman wearing glasses is our teacher.
Students who don't come to class can't sit the exam.

blocks.text: English and French put the description after the noun and start it with a relative word: **the girl who is reading**, la fille qui lit. Turkish puts it before the noun, with no relative word at all, the way English does with a short participle: **the reading girl**.

blocks.title: Pişen or pişmiş?
blocks.text: `-(y)An` describes a noun by what it is doing or did; the `-mIş` adjective of [B1 unit 3](gp-mis-adjective) by the state it is in after a change. *Pişen yemek* is food that is cooking; *pişmiş yemek* is food that has cooked.

A participle takes no personal ending and no tense: *kapıda bekleyen adam*, never *kapıda bekliyor adam*. The verb of the sentence is elsewhere: *Kapıda bekleyen adam* **gitti** (The man who was waiting at the door has left).

Leave out the noun and the participle becomes one: *gelen* (the one who came), *gelenler* (those who came). It then takes plural, case and possessive endings like any noun: *gelenleri* (those who came, as an object), *okuyanlara* (to those who read), *gelenlerin hepsi* (all of those who came).

blocks.caption: *gelenler* (those who came) with case endings
head: Case
Form
Example
rows: *Erken gelenler oturabilir.* Those who come early can sit.
*Geç gelenleri beklemedik.* We didn't wait for the latecomers.
*Gelenlere çay verdik.* We gave tea to those who came.
*Gelenlerden biri Ayşe'ydi.* One of those who came was Ayşe.
*Gelenlerin hepsi gençti.* All of those who came were young.

blocks.text: **With pronouns.** The participle often describes *biri*, *kimse* or *herkes*: *Türkçe bilen biri* (someone who knows Turkish), *Türkçe bilen kimse yok* (there's nobody who knows Turkish), *gelen herkes* (everyone who came). On its own, *Bilen var mı?* asks **Does anyone know?**, literally **Is there one who knows?**

Some have become ordinary nouns: *kazanan* (the winner), *çalışan* (an employee: *şirketin çalışanları*, the company's staff). And you have used one since [A2 unit 1](gp-time-past) without knowing it: *geçen hafta*, **last week**, is **the week that passed**.

items.en: Who won? Who's the winner?
We didn't wait for the latecomers.

items.tr: Burada Türkçe konuşan biri var mı?
items.seg: Burada Türkçe konuş|an biri var mı?
items.en: Is there anyone here who speaks Turkish?
People without a ticket can't go in.
Everyone who took part in the competition was very young.

blocks.text: Rules and notices often speak to **those who…**: *Sınava geç kalanlar giremez* (Those who are late for the exam can't go in), *Bilet almak isteyenler sıraya girsin* (Those who want a ticket should queue).

The noun after the participle can also be the **owner** of the subject: **the child whose father is a doctor**. Inside the clause, the subject takes a possessive ending pointing to that noun, and the verb takes `-(y)An`: *babası doktor olan çocuk*, literally **the child his-father being a doctor**.
A sentence with no verb becomes a participle with *olan* (being), and *var* and *yok* become *olan* and *olmayan*:

head: Sentence
Noun phrase
Meaning
rows: the child whose father is a doctor
my friend whose mother is Turkish
the neighbour who has no car
a room with a window onto the sea
the woman whose cat went missing

items.tr: Babası doktor olan çocuk çok akıllı.
items.seg: Babası doktor ol|an çocuk çok akıllı.
items.en: The child whose father is a doctor is very clever.
We're looking for a house with a garden.

items.tr: Penceresi denize bakan bir oda istiyorum.
items.seg: Penceresi denize bak|an bir oda istiyorum.
items.en: I'd like a room with a sea view.
The woman whose cat went missing is very upset.

items.tr: Arabası olmayan komşumuz her gün otobüse biniyor.
items.seg: Arabası ol|ma|y|an komşumuz her gün otobüse biniyor.
items.en: Our neighbour, who doesn't have a car, takes the bus every day.

blocks.text: English uses **whose** and French dont: the child whose father…, l'enfant dont le père… Turkish needs neither: the possessive ending on *babası* is enough to tie the father to the child.

Don't drop the possessive inside the clause: *babası doktor olan çocuk*, not *baba doktor olan çocuk*. And for simple descriptions, the `-lI` adjectives of [A2 unit 12](gp-li) are often shorter: *bahçeli bir ev*, *sakallı adam*.

In a Turkish noun phrase, everything that describes the noun comes before it, and a participle clause keeps the word order of a sentence, with its verb last. English puts short adjectives first and clauses after; Turkish puts both first.

blocks.caption: Building a noun phrase
head: Turkish
English
rows: an old man running in the park
her sabah parkta koşan yaşlı bir adam
an old man who runs in the park every morning

blocks.text: **The article goes last.** The indefinite *bir* sits right before the noun, or before its last adjective: *parkta koşan bir adam*, *parkta koşan yaşlı bir adam*. Put it in front of the clause and it attaches to the first noun instead: *bir parkta koşan adam* is **the man running in a park**.
**Demonstratives go first.** A demonstrative usually comes first: *bu parkta koşan adam*. That can also mean **the man running in this park**, so to point at the man, say *parkta koşan bu adam*.

**Reading long phrases.** Read up to the noun, find out who or what it is, then go back over the description. In *Annesi Türk olan, İstanbul'da yaşayan ve üç dil konuşan bir arkadaşım var*, the noun is *arkadaşım*: a friend of mine, whose mother is Turkish, who lives in Istanbul and speaks three languages.

items.tr: Parkta koşan yaşlı bir adam gördüm.
items.seg: Parkta koş|an yaşlı bir adam gördüm.
items.en: I saw an old man running in the park.
The young woman sitting in the corner is Selin.
I know a woman who lives in Ankara.

items.tr: Gazete okuyan uzun boylu bir adam gördün mü?
items.seg: Gazete oku|y|an uzun boylu bir adam gördün mü?
items.en: Did you see a tall man reading a newspaper?

blocks.text: Two clauses on one noun are joined with *ve* or a comma, each with its own participle: *Türkçe bilen ve İstanbul'da yaşayan biri* (someone who knows Turkish and lives in Istanbul).

The aorist of [A2 unit 4](gp-aorist-forms) can stand before a noun too, for what something always does or never does: *akar su* (running water), *çalar saat* (a clock that rings: an alarm clock), *çıkmaz sokak* (a street that doesn't come out: a dead end). Turkish no longer builds new ones freely. These are fixed words to learn; for a new description, use `-(y)An`.

head: Word
From
Meaning
rows: döner kebab, meat roasted on a turning spit

blocks.text: Spelling follows the TDK dictionary: some are one word (*akarsu*, *yanardağ*, *okuryazar*), others two (*çalar saat*, *çıkmaz sokak*, *tükenmez kalem*). In speech *tükenmez kalem* is often just *tükenmez*.
Proverbs keep the aorist participle alive: *Görünen köy kılavuz istemez* (The village you can see needs no guide: it's obvious). Here *görünen* is `-(y)An`, and *istemez* the negative aorist.

items.en: Who's the author of this book?
My alarm clock didn't go off this morning.
This street is a dead end.
Do you have a ballpoint pen?
This is a never-ending story.

summary: `-(y)An` turns a verb into an adjective for its subject: *kitap okuyan kız*, *Taksim'e giden otobüs*, *dondurma yiyen çocuk*; negative *gelmeyen*.
The participle has no tense or person; the sentence gives the time: *dün gelen mektup*, *şimdi konuşan kadın*.
Without a noun it is a noun: *gelenler*, *gelenleri*, *gelenlerin hepsi*; with *biri*, *kimse*, *herkes*: *Türkçe bilen biri*.
**Whose**: a possessive on the subject inside the clause, *babası doktor olan çocuk*; *var* and *yok* become *olan* and *olmayan*.
Everything describing a noun comes before it, the clause first, *bir* last: *parkta koşan yaşlı bir adam*.
The aorist participle lives on in fixed words: *yazar*, *çalar saat*, *çıkmaz sokak*, *tükenmez kalem*, *akarsu*.
